IA-BNK-01: If salespeople can push through loans that break the rules, the bank ends up with borrowers who were never going to pay.
IA-BNK-02: Banks are legally required to know who their customers are and to report suspicious activity. Getting this wrong brings fines and, sometimes, criminal charges.
IA-BNK-03: Payments are where money physically leaves the bank, so this is the step a fraudster most wants to control.
IA-BNK-04: If the bank runs out of cash or capital, it stops being a bank. These are the numbers that keep it alive in a bad year.
IA-BNK-05: If the paperwork behind a loan is incomplete, the bank may not be able to enforce it in court when the borrower stops paying.
IA-BNK-06: Security is what the bank falls back on when a loan goes bad. If it was never registered properly or is worth less than recorded, that fallback is not there.
IA-BNK-07: Loan agreements contain promises the borrower must keep. Nobody checking them means the bank misses the early warning that the borrower is in trouble.
IA-BNK-08: The earlier a struggling borrower is handed to specialists, the more money the bank gets back.
IA-BNK-09: Ratings drive how much the loan costs and how much capital the bank must hold. Inflated ratings make the bank look safer than it is.
IA-BNK-10: Lending too much to one customer, or several linked ones, means a single failure can hurt the whole bank. Regulators cap this for good reason.
IA-BNK-11: How risky a customer is decided at the start determines how closely they are watched forever after. Getting it wrong at onboarding is a mistake that persists.
IA-BNK-12: Trade finance and correspondent banking move money across borders in ways that are hard to see through, which is exactly why criminals use them.
IA-BNK-13: When customers are defrauded, the bank often has to reimburse them, and regulators judge how well it protected them.
IA-BNK-14: Companies can be prosecuted for failing to prevent bribery or tax evasion by people acting for them, even if senior management knew nothing.
IA-BNK-15: Branches hold physical cash, and small amounts taken repeatedly add up long before anyone notices.
IA-BNK-16: When payments fail or duplicate, customers lose money and the bank has to make it good, on top of the regulatory attention.
IA-BNK-17: Complaints are the cheapest early warning a bank gets. Ignoring them turns one customer's problem into a redress bill for thousands.
IA-BNK-18: Selling a product to someone it was never designed for eventually means paying them back, often years later and with interest.
IA-INS-01: Every extra pound paid on a claim beyond what the policy requires is profit gone, and it happens quietly across thousands of claims.
IA-INS-02: Brokers and agents sell using the insurer's name, so whatever they do wrong lands on the insurer's desk.
IA-INS-03: Reinsurance is the insurance company's own insurance. If it was set up badly, the company discovers that only when a very large loss arrives.
IA-INS-04: The money set aside for future claims is the single biggest number in an insurer's accounts, and it is an estimate that can be leaned on.
IA-INS-05: Pricing below what the risk deserves wins business today and loses money for years afterwards.
IA-MFG-01: Material that goes in but does not come out as product is money lost. If it is buried in general variances, nobody fixes the cause.
IA-MFG-02: Safety and environmental breaches can shut a plant down, and they injure people. This is not a financial risk first.
IA-RTL-01: Tills are where cash and staff meet thousands of times a day, and a refund against a real sale is the easiest way to take money.
IA-RTL-02: If suppliers under-deliver or overcharge and nobody claims it back, the loss is simply absorbed store by store.
IA-RTL-03: Gift cards and loyalty points are money the business owes customers. Assuming too much of it will never be claimed flatters profit.
IA-AVN-01: An aircraft with incomplete maintenance records cannot legally fly, regardless of whether the work was actually done.
IA-AVN-02: Damage on the ground grounds aircraft and generates claims from airlines, and it is often discovered by the customer rather than the handler.
IA-AVN-03: Leased aircraft must be given back in a specified condition. That bill arrives years after the decisions that caused it.
IA-AVN-04: A ticket sold is not money earned until the passenger flies. Mixing those two up overstates revenue.
IA-AVN-05: Fuel is one of the largest costs an airline has, and nobody stands at the wing checking the litres against the invoice unless someone makes them.
IA-HSP-01: The front desk can give away rooms, discounts and refunds, and each one is money the hotel never sees.
IA-HSP-02: When each property buys locally, prices drift upward and personal relationships creep in.
IA-HSP-03: More drink leaves the bottle than the till records, and the gap is usually explained away as waste.
IA-HSP-04: A room booked through a website can cost so much in commission that the hotel makes almost nothing on it.
IA-ECM-01: An online pricing error is honoured at scale within minutes, before anyone can react.
IA-ECM-02: Customer data is regulated. Keeping it too long or sharing it too widely is a fine, not just a bad look.
IA-ECM-03: Every order picked wrong costs the replacement, the delivery and often the customer.
IA-ECM-04: On a marketplace, the platform is judged by what its sellers list, including counterfeit or unsafe goods.
IA-FMC-01: Distributors buying more than they can sell means the sales figures are not real, and the stock comes back.
IA-FMC-02: If a product batch is unsafe, the company must find every unit fast. Poor traceability turns a problem into a crisis.
IA-FMC-03: Promotional spend is one of the biggest costs in consumer goods, and much of it is paid out against claims nobody checks.
IA-UTL-01: Utility assets carry public safety risk. Deferring maintenance to save money moves the cost to someone's injury.
IA-UTL-02: Cutting off a customer who is ill or in hardship is a regulatory breach and a front-page story.
IA-UTL-03: A utility operates under a licence. Breach its conditions and the regulator, not the market, decides what happens next.
IA-UTL-04: Traders can hide losses by mispricing their own positions, which is why someone independent must value them.
IA-TEL-01: Every call or data session that never reaches billing is a service given away free.
IA-TEL-02: A badly controlled network change can take service down for millions of customers, and that has to be reported to the regulator.
IA-TL-01: Vehicles are valuable and easy to sell cheaply to the wrong person if nobody is watching the disposal.
IA-TL-02: Fuel is easy to take and hard to trace, which makes it one of the most common losses in any fleet business.
IA-TL-03: Skipping maintenance saves money this month and causes breakdowns, accidents and regulator action later.
IA-TL-04: Delivering a shipment and never invoicing it is pure lost revenue, and it does not show up as a variance anywhere.
IA-TL-05: Discounts agreed by salespeople outside their authority quietly erode the margin on multi-year contracts.
IA-TL-06: Buying transport at short notice costs far more than using capacity already under contract.
IA-TL-07: Freight changes hands repeatedly in a terminal, and each handover is an opportunity for it to go missing.
IA-TL-08: Drivers over their legal hours or without valid licences create liability the company cannot insure away.
IA-TL-09: Dangerous goods and customs errors stop shipments and bring penalties, sometimes personal ones.
IA-TL-10: When another carrier moves your freight, their insurance and safety record become your problem.
IA-TL-11: Cargo claims get paid without checking whether another party was actually at fault and should be paying instead.
IA-X-01: Payments to suppliers are the most common route for money to leave a company fraudulently.
IA-X-03: People who change jobs or leave often keep their old system access, which is how small problems become large ones.
IA-X-04: If people do not trust the confidential reporting line, management is the last to know about problems.
IA-X-06: Stock is often the largest number on the balance sheet, and it is only worth what it can actually be sold for.
IA-X-07: Big capital projects get approved on promises, and almost nobody goes back to check whether the promises came true.
IA-X-08: Bank accounts and payment authority are the front door to the company's cash.
IA-X-09: Filing tax late or on the wrong basis costs interest and penalties, and repeats every year until it is fixed.
IA-X-10: Manual journals are how results get adjusted at the last minute, which makes them the first place to look.
IA-X-11: Outsourcing the work never outsources the responsibility. When the supplier fails, it is still your problem.
IA-X-12: Hiring someone without checking who they are, and letting leavers keep access, are both simple failures with expensive consequences.
IA-X-13: How people are paid and promoted drives how they behave, which shapes every other control in the business.
